subject: Bio
title: Disease, breathing & respiration
sub: Pathogens and body defences, lungs and gas exchange, aerobic and anaerobic respiration
strategyIntro: Cambridge Core Biology is assessed on Paper 1 (40 multiple-choice questions, 45 min), Paper 3 (structured theory questions, 1h 15, 80 marks) and Paper 6 (questions on experiments). Your school test may be shorter, but it will be marked the same way.

strategy.title: Multiple choice
points: About a minute per question. If one is taking longer, mark it and move on.
Cross out options you know are wrong first. Two often look similar: read every word.
Never leave one blank. A wrong answer loses nothing.

strategy.title: Structured questions
points: Marks go to keywords. Write the textbook term: “oviduct”, not “tube”.
The marks in brackets tell you how many separate points to make.
Label diagrams with a ruler line that touches the exact part.

strategy.title: Questions on experiments
points: Results tables: units go in the column headings, not next to each number.
Graphs: label both axes with units, choose an even scale, plot with small crosses.
Know the control variables and one safety precaution for each experiment.

strategy.title: Easy marks people lose
points: Mixing up breathing and respiration. Breathing moves air; respiration is a chemical reaction in every cell.
Writing that respiration “makes energy”. It releases energy.
Saying antibiotics work on viruses. They only kill bacteria.
Forgetting the word “anaerobic” means without oxygen, and that in muscles it makes lactic acid, not alcohol.

commandWords: Give a short fact. No explanation needed.
Say what happens or what you see. With data, quote figures and units.
Say why or how. Use “because” and link cause to effect.
Apply what you know to a new situation. Any sensible reason scores.
Give similarities or differences for both things in the same sentence.
Show working and give the unit.
quizIntro: Answer in Paper 1 style: about a minute each, eliminating wrong options first. Read the explanation after every answer, even when you get it right.
flashIntro: These are close to Cambridge’s own wording. Say each definition out loud before you tap, then check you used the exact keywords.

flashcards.back: A disease-causing organism, e.g. a bacterium, virus or fungus.
A disease in which the pathogen can be passed from one host to another.
Passing a pathogen through contact with blood or other body fluids, e.g. HIV.
Passing a pathogen via contaminated surfaces, food, water, the air, or animals such as insects.
Skin and the hairs in the nose stop pathogens getting into the body.
Mucus traps pathogens; stomach acid kills pathogens in food.
Phagocytes engulf and digest pathogens (phagocytosis); lymphocytes make antibodies.
A vaccine contains weakened or dead pathogens (or their antigens). The body makes antibodies, so it can fight the real pathogen quickly later.
Clean water supply, hygienic food preparation, good personal hygiene, safe waste disposal and sewage treatment.
Drugs that kill bacteria. They have no effect on viruses.
Large surface area, thin surface, good blood supply and good ventilation with air.
Tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles where gas exchange happens. Walls one cell thick, surrounded by capillaries.

flashcards.front: Route of air into the lungs
flashcards.back: Nose/mouth → larynx → trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.
C-shaped rings that keep the airway open.
Expired air has less oxygen (about 16% vs 21%), more carbon dioxide (about 4% vs 0.04%) and more water vapour.
Limewater turns milky (cloudy) with carbon dioxide. Expired air turns it cloudy faster than inspired air.
Diaphragm contracts and flattens; intercostal muscles raise the ribs; chest volume increases, so air is drawn in.
Rate and depth of breathing increase, to supply more oxygen and remove more carbon dioxide.
Goblet cells make mucus that traps dust and pathogens; cilia sweep it up to the throat.
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is the chemical reactions in cells that release energy.
Chemical reactions in cells that use oxygen to break down nutrient molecules to release energy.
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
Chemical reactions in cells that break down nutrient molecules to release energy without using oxygen.
glucose → lactic acid
glucose → alcohol (ethanol) + carbon dioxide
Aerobic respiration releases much more energy per glucose molecule than anaerobic.
Muscle contraction, making proteins, cell division, active transport, growth, nerve impulses, keeping body temperature constant.
In the mitochondria.
Carbon dioxide makes bread dough rise; alcohol is made in brewing.
Respiration is controlled by enzymes, so its rate rises with temperature up to an optimum, then falls.

options: A type of white blood cell
quiz.why: A pathogen is the organism that causes disease. The chemicals made by lymphocytes are antibodies.

options: Through contact with infected body fluids
quiz.why: HIV is passed directly in blood and other body fluids, e.g. through sex or shared needles.

quiz.q: Which is a chemical barrier against pathogens?
quiz.why: Stomach acid kills pathogens in food. Skin and nose hairs are mechanical barriers; phagocytes are cells.

quiz.q: Why does treating sewage reduce the spread of disease?
options: It removes pathogens before the water goes back into rivers
quiz.why: Untreated sewage contains pathogens that can get into drinking water. Treatment removes them.

quiz.q: Why are antibiotics not given for flu?
options: Flu is caused by a virus, and antibiotics do not affect viruses
Flu is caused by a bacterium that is too small
quiz.why: Antibiotics kill bacteria only. Using them for viral infections does nothing and helps resistant bacteria spread.

quiz.q: Where does gas exchange take place in the lungs?
quiz.why: The alveoli have thin walls and a huge surface area next to capillaries. The other parts just carry air.

quiz.q: Which shows the approximate composition of expired air?
quiz.why: We use some oxygen (21% → 16%) and add carbon dioxide from respiration (0.04% → 4%).

quiz.q: What is the function of the cartilage rings in the trachea?
quiz.why: Cartilage is stiff, so the trachea does not collapse when air pressure inside falls.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of an efficient gas exchange surface?
quiz.why: A thin surface gives a short diffusion distance. Thick walls would slow diffusion.

quiz.q: Why do breathing rate and depth increase during exercise?
options: Muscles respire more and need more oxygen; more carbon dioxide must be removed
quiz.why: Working muscles respire faster, so more oxygen must be taken in and more carbon dioxide breathed out.

quiz.q: What are the products of aerobic respiration?
quiz.why: Glucose and oxygen are the reactants; carbon dioxide and water are the products.

quiz.q: During hard exercise, anaerobic respiration in muscles produces:
quiz.why: Muscles make lactic acid. Yeast makes alcohol and carbon dioxide.
Yeast respires the sugar, and bubbles of carbon dioxide make the dough expand.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT use energy from respiration?
quiz.why: Diffusion is passive: it uses the particles’ own kinetic energy, not energy from respiration.

quiz.q: Germinating seeds in a vacuum flask make the temperature inside rise. Why?
options: Respiration releases energy, some as heat
quiz.why: Respiring cells release energy; some is lost as heat, which the flask traps. Boiled (dead) seeds give a control.

examIntro: Paper 3 style. Write your answer first, then open the mark scheme and give yourself one mark per point you made clearly. One point per mark is the rule.

exam.q: State two ways a pathogen can be transmitted indirectly.
points: Contaminated surfaces
Contaminated food
Contaminated water
Through the air (droplets)
By animals / insect vectors

exam.q: Describe three ways the body stops pathogens getting in, or kills them before they cause disease.
points: Skin acts as a barrier
Hairs in the nose trap particles
Mucus traps pathogens
Stomach acid kills pathogens in food
Phagocytes engulf pathogens
Lymphocytes make antibodies

exam.q: Explain how vaccination protects a person from a disease.
points: The vaccine contains weakened / dead pathogens or their antigens
White blood cells (lymphocytes) make antibodies
Memory cells are made
If the real pathogen enters, antibodies are made faster / in larger amounts
The pathogen is destroyed before the person becomes ill

exam.q: State two features of alveoli that make gas exchange efficient.
points: Large surface area (many alveoli)
Thin walls (one cell thick)
Good blood supply / surrounded by capillaries
Well ventilated
Moist surface

exam.q: Describe three differences between inspired and expired air.
points: Expired air has less oxygen (21% → 16%)
Expired air has more carbon dioxide (0.04% → 4%)
Expired air has more water vapour
Expired air is warmer
exam.note: Any 3. Compare both, e.g. “expired air has more…”.

exam.q: Explain how oxygen gets from the air in an alveolus into the blood, and how the alveoli are adapted for this.
points: Oxygen moves by diffusion
From higher concentration in the alveolus to lower concentration in the blood
Across thin walls of alveolus and capillary (short distance)
Many alveoli give a large surface area
Good blood supply carries oxygen away, keeping the gradient steep
Ventilation brings in fresh air, keeping oxygen concentration high
Oxygen combines with haemoglobin in red blood cells

exam.q: Write the word equation for aerobic respiration.
points: glucose + oxygen (on the left)
→ carbon dioxide + water (on the right)

exam.q: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in human muscles.
points: Aerobic uses oxygen; anaerobic does not
Aerobic makes carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic makes lactic acid
Aerobic releases much more energy (per glucose)
Both break down glucose / both release energy
exam.note: Any 3. Each point must refer to both types.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to find how temperature affects the rate of respiration of yeast. Include the result you would expect.
points: Mix yeast with sugar solution
Put tubes in water baths at different temperatures
Count bubbles / measure volume of carbon dioxide in a set time
Keep the same mass of yeast, volume and concentration of sugar solution
Repeat at each temperature and take a mean
Rate increases with temperature up to an optimum (around 35–40 °C)
Then falls as enzymes are denatured
